city.name: Shibuya
city.description: Sangenjaya to Shibuya, Harajuku and Yoyogi Park from open data, lit by the real sun: Project PLATEAU's surveyed heights, the scramble and Hachiko, SHIBUYA SKY 229 m up, Center Gai, Shibuya Stream and the streets Persona 5 drew.

tour.title: Sangenjaya to Harajuku, from open data
tour.text: {buildings} buildings. {share:plateau}% of the footprint area stands at a height that Project PLATEAU surveyed, on GSI's laser-scanned bare earth under GSI aerial photographs.

tour.title: The scramble
tour.text: Four streets meet at Shibuya's scramble, and when the lights change every crossing goes green at once, the diagonal too. The white bars are drawn from OpenStreetMap's crosswalks. Hachiko sits on his granite to the south.

tour.title: SHIBUYA SKY, 229 m
tour.text: On Scramble Square's roof (2019): about 2,500 m² of open deck at {landmark:shibuya_sky.deck_m} m, glass at the edge, GEO COMPASS in the middle and the escalator coming up out of the 46th floor.

tour.title: Sangenjaya's triangle
tour.text: Between Setagaya-dori and Route 246, the backstreets of Sangenjaya: a bathhouse, a snack bar, a meat shop open all night. A game drew its home town here and called it Yongen-Jaya.

protection.title: No sun-access rule for public places
protection.summary: Tokyo protects no park's sunlight. The windows are a lunch-hour thought experiment for this project, as in the Marunouchi model.
protection.source_note: Windows are our own choice (noon to 13:00, all year), not law. The Building Standards Act's shadow rule (日影規制, art. 56-2) limits hours of shadow on neighbouring land in residential-type zones; it does not cover public places and does not apply in commercial districts such as Shibuya.
protection.reading_note: Tokyo keeps standard time all year. Miyashita Park is a roof garden on a mall (2020): its sun here is read at the ground, so treat it with care.
protection.tip: Tip: try a tower on the block south of Yoyogi Park, west of Harajuku Station.

light_show.name: CROSSING LIGHT
light_show.note: SHIBUYA SKY's 18 searchlights: shows from 19:00 on the hour and the half hour, to 22:00 (enjoytokyo, nippon.com). Each show's length and the beams' movement here are illustrative.

shore.encoding: r: 128 + 2 x signed distance to the shoreline (m, water positive); g: sand; b: rock

trees.note: Species are not mapped; the mix is a guess from the cities' street-tree surveys and the parks' own guides: ginkgo and zelkova (keyaki) are Japan's commonest street trees, with plane trees and camphor; the woods are the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves and camphors, with zelkovas, black pines, maples and a few cedars (sugi, standing for hinoki too). Areas give the parks and precincts known for their own trees a mix of their own; their outlines are OpenStreetMap's (pipeline/tree_areas.py).

areas.name: Hachiko Square
areas.note: Hachiko Square: cherries in the round planters and a maple behind Hachiko. The shared trees have no cherry; a spreading zelkova stands in for it

areas.name: Meiji Jingu
areas.note: The planted shrine forest, now mostly camphor and the evergreen oaks and shii of the laurel forest.

signs.note: shop signs on street fronts in the districts; indicative, not the real shops' signs

sources.places: Overture base land use (OpenStreetMap, ODbL); rules: No sun-access rule for public places
sources.trees: Overture base land, tree points and rows (OpenStreetMap, ODbL); heights not mapped
sources.landmarks: SHIBUYA SKY from SHIBUYA SKY and Wikipedia (229 m, 2,500 m², 18 searchlights, 360 m/min lifts); the scramble's screens at their operators' published sizes; Yoyogi National Gymnasium from OpenStreetMap and Tange's drawings. Signs, screens and shop fronts are indicative.
